#### Composing a target instead of naming one

`--compose-cli
ent <id-or-name>` builds an execution stack for this run instead of\nnaming a saved environment, refined by `--compose-computer`,
`--compose-model`,\n`--compose-server-group`, `--compose-skill` and `--compose-secret`. The stack becomes an unnamed,\ncontent-add
ressed environment (the same one `environments ensure-adhoc`\nproduces), so composing the same stack twice reuses one environment.

`--compose-host` is the deprecated spelling of the same flag.

`--compose-model` and `--compose-secret` carry the deployment r
equirement\ndescribed under [Deployment support for model overrides and secret\ngrants](#deployment-support-for-model-overrides-an
d-secret-grants): a launch that names\neither is refused before it composes anything if this deployment does not\npublish the capa

bility.

> [!WARNING]
>
> **With `--save-targets`, this edits the suite.** The composed environment is
> appended to the suit
e's environment list — deliberately, because an\n> environment the suite does not list is one nobody can re-run from the app\n> af
terwards. Without it the stack is ephemeral and the suite is untouched,\n> except on a deployment with no ephemeral-launch support
, where a\n`--wait` it exits **4** (see the exit-code table above). A per-target failure\ndoes not abort its siblings, so exiting

0 would let a pipeline read "1 of 3
runs never started" as a clean launch.

#### `--file`: upload and run a suite file

`ev
al run --file` reads the versioned suite file (`schemaVersion: \"1\"`),\nauthenticates, then validates. A contract-invalid file ex
its **2** after the\nauth request — it does not start a run. `eval validate` on the same bytes\nstill exits 1: that command is a v

erdict on the file; this one is not.

The file's `suite.id` is the declared suite identity. The first run creates a
file-owned
suite stamped with that id; later runs of the same id in the same\nproject update that suite rather than creating a second one. A

UI-authored
suite has no declared id, so no file can claim it. Resolve is never by name.

File `passThreshold` is a fraction; t
he hosted suite grades on a percent. The\nconversion refuses rather than approximates. A file count above **10**\n(`repetitions` i

n a `schemaVersion: "1"` file, `iterations` in `"2"`) is
refused by name (`REPETITIONS_CAP`) and is not clamped.

**Which v
ocabulary the sync speaks is the deployment's call.** Before writing\nanything, the CLI reads `GET /capabilities` once. A deployme
nt that advertises\n`vocabulary.version: 2` gets every request with `x-mcpjam-eval-vocabulary: 2`\nand case bodies spelled canonic
ally — `iterations` (the exact count),\n`legacyIterations` (the legacy floor, the same number) and `assertions` —\ninstead of `rep
etitions` / `iterations` / `checks`. A deployment without the\ncapability block, or without the capabilities route at all, is spok
en to in\nvocabulary 1, byte-for-byte as before. Nothing in the file changes either way:\nthe dialect of the file and the vocabula

ry of the wire are independent.

Cases are synced in batches of at most 100 (`create_eval_cases`). Every
declared case is creat
ed or updated, including `disabled: true` rows. A case\nthe file **no longer declares** is deleted from the hosted suite before\nl
aunch. A case the file still declares but marks `disabled: true` is **kept,\nwith its history** — it is simply left out of the lau

nch, so parking a flaky
test does not destroy its past results and re-enabling it later resumes the
same case.
The run is scope
d to the enabled cases either way. A file with no enabled\ncases is refused (`NO_ENABLED_CASES`) rather than launching the whole\n
persisted suite. `--case` may only name an enabled case. A later run updates\nexisting cases by declared id and creates new ones.
An enabled case that\noverrides `passThreshold` is refused: hosted grading is suite-wide. A\ndisabled case with the same override
is ignored, matching how repetitions\nare checked. Authored\n`defaults.toolPolicy` and non-empty `defaults.validity` gates are ref
used at\nhosted CLI launch (`TOOL_POLICY_UNSUPPORTED` / the corresponding validity\nrefusal). Hosted platform-authored suites do n
ot currently have a backend\ntool-policy field or enforcement path, so the CLI does not upload a suite that\nwould claim those gua
rantees. When supported by an eval runner, `toolPolicy`\nis enforced at execution time with denied tools kept visible but blocked;
\nserver annotations are advisory and **UNTRUSTED**. The file's default count\n(`defaults.repetitions`, or `defaults.iterations` i
n `schemaVersion: \"2\"`) is\ninherited per case and is not uploaded as a suite `minIterations` floor.\nAuthored `defaults.systemP
rompt` and `defaults.temperature` are uploaded as\nexecution defaults; omitted fields stay omitted so the platform applies its\now
n defaults. `target.hosts` and `target.environment` are attached before\nlaunch. A file environment takes precedence over file hos
ts for that launch,\nwhile an explicit CLI target takes precedence over both. When an explicit CLI\ntarget is provided (for exampl
e `--host`), the file's `target.hosts` are\n**not** synchronized to the suite's persisted host attachments — the suite\nkeeps what
ever hosts it already has. Host attachment synchronization only\nruns when no explicit CLI target overrides the file. Environment

attachment
synchronization is unaffected and always runs.

Without `--idempotency-key`, the CLI mints a fresh UUID for every in
vocation\nand prints it to stderr before launch (`Eval idempotency key: <key>`). Each\ninvocation therefore starts and bills a new
run. To retry a launch whose\nresponse was lost — without starting a second run — pass the key that was\nprinted: `--idempotency-

key <printed-key>`. A replay is marked `deduped` in
the receipt and human output. `--notes` is not part of the key.

##### Impo
rted cases: live tool resolution, and per-run approval\n\nEvery file run performs the same live check `eval validate --project` pe
rforms,\n**before it writes anything**. It is not opt-in and there is no flag to skip\nit. A file with no deterministic `toolCall`

steps asks no question and pays no
round trip.

What happens when a deterministic reference does not resolve depends on the
c

ase:

| Case | Outcome |
| - | - |
| Selected (enabled, and named by `--case` if you used it) | The launch **refuses before th
e suite is synced** — nothing is written and nothing is billed |\n| Imported, not selected | Its claim is rewritten to `unresolved
` (keeping `sourceCaseKey`) and it is **still persisted**, so the hosted record says what MCPJam found rather than still asserting
a claim about a missing tool |\n| Native, not selected | Left exactly as authored. A hand-written case never acquires an `import`
block from this — \"somebody wrote this\" and \"something converted this\" are different facts |\n\nEach target is checked on **i
ts own** server set. `--host` is checked against\nthat host's configured servers rather than the file's, because that is the set\n
the run connects — validating `target.servers` would approve a tool the host\ncannot reach. A host the FILE declares uses its own
`servers` list when it\ndeclares one (those are attached to the host before launch) and the host's\nconfigured set when the field
is omitted. An explicitly empty `servers: []`\nis a real, empty set — it clears the attachment before launch — and is\nvalidated a
